name: Job's three friends
charge: Speaking of God the thing that is not right; condemning the righteous
summary: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite made an appointment together to come and mourn with Job and to comfort him. They wept, rent their mantles, and sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights without a word. Then they argued for thirty chapters that his suffering proved hidden sin, and Eliphaz at last invented the sins outright. When the Lord answered out of the whirlwind he answered them too, and required them to bring sacrifice to the man they had condemned.
offense: Their first response was compassion. They heard of the evil that was come upon him and came every one from his own place, having made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him (Job 2:11); they wept, rent their mantles, and sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him, for they saw  that his grief was very great (Job 2:12-13). Their presence in his grief was not itself the fault. The fault is in what they concluded and would not abandon. Eliphaz began from a rule that is not always true: who ever perished, being innocent, or where were the righteous cut off (Job 4:7). Bildad argued from God's justice to Job's guilt, doth God pervert judgment, or doth the Almighty pervert justice (Job 8:3), which is a true question put to a false use. Zophar spoke a heavy precept and misapplied it, that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth (Job 11:6), treating unproved guilt as something already established. Then Eliphaz stopped
judgment: My wrath is kindled against thee and against thy two friends, for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath. They were ordered to bring seven bullocks and seven rams to Job and have him pray for them, lest I deal with you after your folly. He did, and the Lord accepted Job.

entries.commentary: Job answers the Most High and confesses that He can do everything and that no thought can be withholden from Him. This is a little thing in the scriptures to take heed to: the Most High hears our words and our thoughts, so the hatred or the private spirit a man carries cannot be hidden from Him. He knows the inward parts of men. Job says he uttered what he understood not, things too wonderful for him which he knew not. He had heard of the Most High by the hearing of the ear, but now his eye sees Him, and therefore he abhors himself and repents in dust and ashes. Dust and ashes refer to the custom our forefathers had of putting ashes on the head as a sign of sorrow and repentance. -

After the Most High had spoken these words, He tells Eliphaz the Temanite that His wrath is kindled against him and his two friends, because they have not spoken of Him the thing that is right, as His servant Job has. Throughout the book Job's three friends dealt wrongly with him after his children were killed and everything was taken, so they did not deal righteously as their brother Job did. He commands them to take seven bullocks and seven rams and go to Job and offer a burnt offering for themselves, and Job will pray for them, for him will He accept, lest He deal with them after their folly. The sacrifice for their sin had to be brought to Job, the righteous one in the situation. This is how the priesthood worked, all the way from Leviticus and the five books throughout history: we brought the sacrifice to the Levites and priests and they did it on our behalf, and if a man did not bring his sacrifice, the Most High would deal with him and what he did would not be forgiven. Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did as the Most High commanded, and He accepted Job. -

The Most High turned the captivity of Job when he prayed for his friends, and gave him twice as much as he had before. It was not the prayer alone that availed, but the prayer of a righteous man, so the Most High deals with those that are dealing in righteousness. Then all his brethren, sisters, and former acquaintances came and ate bread with him, bemoaned him, and comforted him over all the evil the Most High had brought upon him, and every man gave him a piece of money and an earring of gold. After his captivity was turned his friends returned as well. -

The Most High blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning: fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she asses, along with seven sons and three daughters. He named the daughters Jemima, Kezia, and Keren-happuch, and in all the land were no women found so fair, and their father gave them inheritance among their brethren. Job lived a hundred and forty years after this and saw his sons and his sons' sons, even four generations, and died being old and full of days. He received much more than he had in the beginning, all because he stayed faithful to the Most High through the whole trial. The purpose of the trial was to see whether Job would fix himself and stay faithful or curse the Most High. The same thing happens to us: we endure to the end as Job did, and at some point the Most High will turn the captivity of the Israelites who kept the commandments and repay them for all their righteousness, far more than double the houses, families, cars, and jobs we have now, giving us much more in the kingdom. -
Job responds to what his friends think they know. He tells them the knowledge you think you have, I myself already know, and I am not inferior unto you in understanding.

Job desires to speak to the Almighty and to reason with God directly, not with these friends. He calls them forgers of lies and physicians of no value, because the things they are trying to tell him cannot help him. In verse 5 he is basically telling them to shut up. If they would hold their tongue that would be wisdom in the sight of the Most High, because the things they speak are not true and Job is not ignorant of what is being done to him by the hand of God.

Job warns his friends about speaking wickedly for God and talking deceitfully for Him, accepting God's person to defend their own accusations. He asks whether it is good that God should search them out. If they secretly accept persons and mock God, His excellency will make them afraid and His dread will fall upon them. Their remembrance is like ashes, their bodies like bodies of clay.

Job tells them to hold their peace and let him alone to speak, and let come on him what will. He is content to let whatever is going to happen to him happen by the hand of God. Though he take his flesh in his teeth and put his life in his hand, though God slay him, yet will he trust in Him and maintain his own ways before Him. God also shall be his salvation, for a hypocrite shall not come before Him.
Job asks them to hear his speech diligently. He has ordered his cause and knows that he shall be justified. He asks who will plead with him, for if he holds his tongue he shall give up the ghost.

Job asks God for only two things: withdraw His hand from him, and let not His dread make him afraid. Then let God call and Job will answer, or let Job speak and God answer him. He asks God to make him know how many are his iniquities and sins. Job is pleading with the Most High to show him what sin he is in, if he is in sin at all, for the things he is going through.

Job asks why God hides His face and holds him for an enemy. He feels broken like a leaf driven to and fro and dry stubble pursued. He says God writes bitter things against him and makes him possess the iniquities of his youth, putting his feet in stocks and setting a print upon the heels of his feet, while he consumes away as a rotten and moth-eaten garment.

Then Eliphaz the Temanite answers: can a man be profitable unto God, as he that is wise is profitable to himself? Is it any pleasure to the Almighty that you are righteous, or gain that you make your ways perfect? Will he reprove you for fear of you? Will he enter with you into judgment? Is not your wickedness great and your iniquity infinite? Eliphaz throws Job's righteousness back as filthy rags, as if keeping the commandments profits nothing. But Christ told us if we keep the commandments and follow him, we will rule on thrones with him, so there is falsehood in Eliphaz's answer. -

Eliphaz accuses Job: you have taken a pledge from your brother for naught and stripped the naked of their clothing, withheld water from the weary and bread from the hungry, sent widows away empty, and broken the arms of the fatherless. Therefore snares are round about you, and sudden fear troubleth you. Eliphaz claims Job's suffering proves Job was sinning, but the Lord was only trying him. The truth is the opposite: when Job had his riches he dealt righteously, helped people, taught people, and was looked up to like an elder in the city. -

Is not God in the height of heaven? Behold the height of the stars, how high they are. And you say, how doth God know? Can he judge through the dark cloud? Thick clouds are a covering to him that he seeth not, and he walketh in the circuit of heaven. Eliphaz says God is surrounded by thick clouds and cannot judge through them, but that is when God is really looking, when you think he is not. -

Have you marked the old way which wicked men have trodden, which were cut down out of time, whose foundation was overthrown with a flood? This points to the men destroyed in the flood. They said unto God, depart from us, and what can the Almighty do for them, yet he filled their houses with good things. But the counsel of the wicked is far from Job. The righteous see it and are glad, and the innocent laugh them to scorn, while their substance is not cut down but the remnant of them the fire consumes.

Acquaint now thyself with him and be at peace; thereby good shall come unto thee. You do not acquaint yourself with God by whispering that you love him; you hear from God through his prophets and his people to whom he gave his word. Receive the law from his mouth and lay up his words in your heart. If you return to the Almighty you shall be built up and put away iniquity far from your tabernacle. This was our job, to build up our people. -

Then you shall have your delight in the Almighty and lift up your face unto God. You shall make your prayer unto him and he shall hear you, for he hears you when you keep the commandments. You shall pay your vow, the original agreement you made in the covenant to keep his commandments. You shall decree a thing and it shall be established, and the light shall shine upon your ways. When men are cast down you shall say there is lifting up, and he shall save the humble person. He shall deliver the island of the innocent, delivered by the pureness of your hands.

A lot of us think, well, I did not do nothing wrong, so why is this happening to me, why me? That is a common fleshly response to a lot of things we go through, but we have to take a step back and see who is in control of everything and for what purpose. Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered: if we assay to commune with thee, wilt thou be grieved? But who can withhold himself from speaking? Eliphaz is like, you go to visit somebody that is sick and you do not want to say the wrong thing, but we just cannot sit here and say nothing. Behold, thou hast instructed many, and thou hast strengthened the weak hands; thy words have upholden him that was falling, and thou hast strengthened the feeble knees. But now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest; it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled. That right there cuts deep. A lot of times we can give other people the scriptures, First Corinthians 10:13, Ecclesiasticus chapter 2, [Deuteronomy 28](/bible/deuteronomy/28), and be the strongest person out there. But then as soon as a trial comes to us, that is when we fall apart. That is what Eliphaz was asking: now trial is coming to you, Job, and now you are falling apart. Is not this thy fear, thy confidence, thy hope, and the uprightness of thy ways? Eliphaz is saying, you used to uplift people, and now trouble is coming upon you and you are about to lose your mind. Maybe you did something. Sometimes it is something we did, but a lot of times it is not; it is for us to go through something because we can handle it, and be a shining example to the next person.

Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? Or where were the righteous cut off? Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same. By the blast of God they perish, and by the breath of his nostrils are they consumed. The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the fierce lion, and the teeth of the young lions, are broken. The old lion perisheth for lack of prey, and the stout lion's whelps are scattered abroad.

Now a thing was secretly brought to me, and mine ear received a little thereof. In thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falleth on men. Now it is talking about the dreams that we have. Fear came upon me, and trembling, which made all my bones to shake. Then a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up. It stood still, but I could not discern the form thereof; an image was before mine eyes, there was silence, and I heard a voice. Saying, shall mortal man be more just than God? Shall a man be more pure than his maker? Behold, he put no trust in his servants, and his angels he charged with folly. How much less in them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, which are crushed before the moth? They are destroyed from morning to evening; they perish for ever without any regarding it. Doth not their excellency which is in them go away? They die, even without wisdom. Eliphaz is basically telling Job, maybe it is something that you did, something you got going on, something you need to examine yourself with. And that is where it ends. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement)

Bildad the Shuhite answers: how long will Job speak these things, and how long shall the words of his mouth be like a strong wind? He accuses Job of just talking on and on. Does God pervert judgment, or does the Almighty pervert justice? Bildad asks if Job is claiming God is being unjust, picking on a man so righteous. If Job's children sinned against Him, He cast them away for their transgression. This points back to Job's children celebrating their days, whom Job sanctified because he knew they might have sinned.

If Job would seek unto God early and make supplication to the Almighty, and if he were pure and upright, then God would awake for him and make the habitation of his righteousness prosperous. Though his beginning was small, his latter end should greatly increase. Bildad promises restoration, but on the false premise that Job is not already upright. -

Inquire of the former age and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers, for we are but of yesterday and know nothing, our days upon earth being a shadow. Shall not they teach thee and tell thee and utter words out of their heart? This is what we do in this truth: search our history, go back into the scriptures, learn our mistakes and our names, and walk in the spirit of strength and prophecy the fathers had.

Can the rush grow up without mire, or the flag grow without water? These are plants by the water; without their source they wither before any other herb while still in their greenness. So are the paths of all that forget God, and the hypocrite's hope shall perish. His hope shall be cut off and his trust shall be a spider's web; any strong thing breaks through it, for it has no foundation. He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand; he shall hold it fast, but it shall not endure, because there is no foundation in the one who forgets God.

The wicked is green before the sun, his branch shooting forth in his garden, his roots wrapped about the heap and seeing the place of stones. But if he is destroyed from his place, it shall deny him, saying it never saw him. This is the joy of his way, and out of the earth shall others grow in his place.

God will not cast away a perfect man, neither will He help the evildoers. He will yet fill Job's mouth with laughing and his lips with rejoicing. They that hate Job shall be clothed with shame, and the dwelling place of the wicked shall come to nought. Bildad concludes that Job must present his case, for God is a just judge who does what is right to whom it is right. In the chapters to come Job will present his case and the Most High will give His answer. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high)

Zophar the Naamathite answers and asks whether the multitude of words should be left unanswered and whether a man full of talk should be justified. He asks whether Job's lies should make men hold their peace, and whether when Job mocks no man shall make him ashamed. Job has said his doctrine is pure and he is clean in God's eyes, and Zophar is mocking that. Zophar wishes that God would speak and open his lips against Job and show him the secrets of wisdom, that they are double to that which is known; only when the Most High opens your eyes and reveals the secrets of wisdom will you understand. Zophar says God exacteth of Job less than his iniquity deserves; this is a heavy precept, because it means the Most High gives us less than we deserve, so Job has a lot of mercy on him even though he cannot see it. Even so, Job questioned but he did not curse God.

Canst thou by searching find out God? Canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection? It is as high as heaven, what canst thou do; deeper than hell, what canst thou know. The measure thereof is longer than the earth and broader than the sea; you cannot go high enough, wide enough, or low enough to find out the perfection of God. This is where the song ain't no mountain high enough comes from. If the Most High cut off, shut up, or gather together, then who can hinder him? He knoweth vain men and seeth wickedness; will he not then consider it? Vain man would be wise, though man be born like a wild ass's colt.

Zophar tells Job to prepare his heart and stretch out his hands toward the Most High. If iniquity be in thy hand, put it far away, and let not wickedness dwell in thy tabernacles; this is Job speaking to us as well, to put off the uncleanliness, the wickedness, the impure minds and ways we had in the world. Not letting wickedness dwell in thy tabernacle means the temple, the spirit here, purifying yourself and dedicating it back to the Most High, reforming your mind on a daily basis. Then shalt thou lift up thy face without spot; yea, thou shalt be steadfast and shalt not fear. Thou shalt forget thy misery and remember it as waters that pass away.

Thine age shall be clearer than the noonday; thou shalt shine forth and be as the morning. Thou shalt be secure because there is hope; thou shalt dig about thee and take thy rest in safety. Thou shalt lie down and none shall make thee afraid; yea, many shall make suit unto thee. But the eyes of the wicked shall fail; they shall not escape, and their hope shall be as the giving up of the ghost, which is the breath that leaves the body when they die.

verses.text: And it was so, that after the Lord had spoken these words unto Job, the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath.

Therefore take unto you now seven bullocks and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and offer up for yourselves a burnt offering; and my servant Job shall pray for you: for him will I accept: lest I deal with you after your folly, in that ye have not spoken of me the thing which is right, like my servant Job.
So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went, and did according as the Lord commanded them: the Lord also accepted Job.
Will ye speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him?
Will ye accept his person? will ye contend for God?
Is it good that he should search you out? or as one man mocketh another, do ye so mock him?
He will surely reprove you, if ye do secretly accept persons.
Is not thy wickedness great? and thine iniquities infinite?
For thou hast taken a pledge from thy brother for nought, and stripped the naked of their clothing.
Thou hast not given water to the weary to drink, and thou hast withholden bread from the hungry.
But as for the mighty man, he had the earth; and the honourable man dwelt in it.
Thou hast sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless have been broken.
Therefore snares are round about thee, and sudden fear troubleth thee;
Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?
Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same.
If thou wouldest seek unto God betimes, and make thy supplication to the Almighty;
If thou wert pure and upright; surely now he would awake for thee, and make the habitation of thy righteousness prosperous.
And that he would shew thee the secrets of wisdom, that they are double to that which is! Know therefore that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth.

lawsResolved.text: Doing injustice by justifying the wicked and condemning the righteous is an abomination and condemned by God.
We should not speak evil of someone out of suspicions or assumptions.
You shall not lie to one another.
Do not be a witness against your neighbor without cause.
Do not judge others lest you be judged yourselves, for in the way you judge, you will be judged.
